idiom_name: object with fixed inline storage, a spilled heap form and a discriminator
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the type one storage region sized for the common case and one for the general case, plus a discriminator that says which is live, and route every operation through accessors so the rest of the type never learns which representation is in use. Put the transition in a single spill operation and keep the small path allocation-free, so constructing, copying, moving and destroying a small value cannot fail or throw. Derive the inline capacity from the measured payload-size distribution, keep it private, and document the invalidation rules, because a spill or a move relocates the payload.
pitfalls: Skipping the discriminator and inferring the state from the data (len > N, pointer range) breaks for empty or exactly-at-capacity values.
Letting the construction path write the payload directly while the access path reads through the other representation - keep construction inside the same accessors.
Choosing the inline capacity by taste instead of by distribution: too small and everything spills, too large and every copy pays.

Assuming every mature implementation adopts it: Rust's String is deliberately heap-only (pointer/length/capacity, 24 bytes) because API promises like into_bytes and as_mut_vec hand out the underlying byte vector - where the public contract transfers buffer ownership, an inline representation is a liability, not an optimization.

Embedding the buffer in an object that is itself heap-allocated or stored densely: LLVM's own guidance is that the inline region makes SmallVector's sizeof large so 'you don't want to allocate lots of them' - the inline region pays where it sits on the stack or inside a long-lived object, not inside every container that holds one.
